Maladaptive Strategies.value: never allow myself to feel or express anger
Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark).
avoid anything that could be stressful

Threat.value: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger
I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place

Memory.value: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time
When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

vignette: Dat Nguyen was seventy-two when he finally sat across from a clinician, his hands folded tightly over his knees. The memory that had brought him there did not arrive as a coherent story. It arrived as a sudden, suffocating weight behind his ribs. Fifty years earlier, in a cramped second-floor apartment in Houston, his former partner had grabbed him by the collar and hurled him against the wall. The ceiling light shattered on impact. In the pitch black, his partner's footsteps had circled him, heavy and unpredictable, before a heavy hand came down on his shoulder. Dat had pressed himself against the floorboards, knees drawn to his chest, arms wrapped over his head, waiting for the next strike. He never fought back. He had come to believe that anger was a dangerous spark in a room that only needed more fire. He swallowed every flare of rage, smoothing his features into placid calm whenever the memories tried to surface. Over the decades, those years in the dark did not fade into ordinary recollection. The accounts of the violence settled into his nervous system like old frost. When Dat recalled the event now, it carried the same terror he had felt in that room, and his body automatically curled back into the defensive posture he had held for so long. He was certain that the past was not entirely his own anymore; the accounts of the violence felt like they belonged to a stranger who had worn his life. He simply endured the flashbacks. He refused to let himself feel or express anger. He held anger, he knew, to be a dangerous spark in a room that only needed more fire. His life had rearranged itself around these unseen thresholds. Over months, he began to map his daily routes to avoid unlit stairwells. He told the hiring family he needed fewer hours, then fewer days. He avoided anything that could be stressful. When the household budget grew tight, he refused to sit at the kitchen table with the bills. When neighbors complained about noise, he quietly packed his bags rather than confront the issue. The consequences accumulated quietly. The mother stopped asking about his shifts, adjusting the nursery schedule around his preferences. His wife stopped inviting him to evening gatherings. His body never rested. Even when he knew he was in a safe place, in his own well-furnished home, he was unable to relax. His shoulders stayed raised, his breathing shallow, as if the dark apartment were still just around the corner. Dat took the position as a nanny for a young family in suburban Atlanta to fill his days with predictable routines. The work provided structure, but it also placed him in environments that constantly triggered his alert systems. He never allowed himself to feel or express anger when the toddler beside him dropped a wooden block with a loud clap. Instead, his startle response flared instantly. His muscles locked, and he would turn his head sharply, already bracing. Unexpected movement nearby caused him to react as if he were in danger. He flinched when the mother reached past him to retrieve a toy, his pulse racing until he recognized her calm smile. He knew the nursery was safe. He knew the gates were latched. But he was unable to relax even when he knew he was in a safe place. His mind tracked the child's every shift, his body coiled tight, waiting for a threat that had already passed. What frightened him most was not the present, but the sudden return of the old terror. He had tried to build a life that required no confrontation, no uncertainty, no sudden darkness. Yet the memories persisted, unbidden and alien. What finally brought him to seek help was the exhaustion of constantly holding himself rigid. He was most afraid of losing the fragile peace he had constructed, but he hoped, quietly, to learn how to let his shoulders drop. He wanted to walk into a room without scanning the corners, and to sit with his wife without his hands trembling. He did not know how to explain that the fight had ended decades ago, only that his body kept waiting for the next blow.
